source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC3767417 (author manuscript of Am J Psychiatry 2010;167(8):969-976), read in full in my own browser tab; Tables 1 and 2 read as HTML tables; the survival-curve figures (Figures 1-3) carry no number used by the claims and were not needed

claims.overstatement: The sentence that the dependence hazard ratios 'mostly reflect men's higher chance of ever becoming dependent, not faster progression' is the editors' inference, stated as fact. The authors read the same survival curves and a significant cohort x gender x time interaction (F = 54.08, p<0.01) the other way: men reached dependence faster than women, more so in recent cohorts. The inference fits Table 1 (similar mean times overall; 23.7% of men vs 16.2% of women who drank became dependent, my arithmetic), but the claim should label it as the editors' reading and report the authors' reading. Minor: the 38,309 are lifetime drinkers as the surveys define them (more than 12 drinks ever), not everyone who had ever drunk.
claims.note: Every Keyes number in the statement and magnitude checks: response rates 90% and 81%; n 53,238 (cohort ns sum to it); 38,309; 19.0 vs 17.8; gaps 3.0 and 0.4 (my subtraction); all ten hazard ratios and intervals; 5.6 vs 5.8 with ratio 1.04, not significant; 3.7 vs 4.2 with p = 0.02; 5.5 vs 6.4 not marked, and my t from the printed means and SEs is 2.40, which matches the card's approximation of about 2.4; 19.4 vs 23.5; and the totals 6.1 vs 7.0 really cannot be averages of the cohort rows (n-weighted row means about 14.8 and 13.2). Adjustment set: the Methods text says age was tested and dropped, but Table 2's footnote a, and the Results paragraph on the two-way interaction, list age among the controls. The claim follows the Methods text and should note the conflict or add age. The claim is right that the Discussion's statement that women were faster on neither step goes beyond Table 1 (cohort 2 dependence p = 0.02; cohort 5 treatment p = 0.002; total treatment marked p<0.05). Telescoping studies measured timing among people who reached each step, while the hazards here are among everyone at risk; the claim keeps the two apart correctly.

anchors.locator: Method › Sources of Data, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Two cross-sectional US national surveys using the same interview (AUDADIS-IV): NLAES 1991–1992 (response 90%) and NESARC 2001–2002 (response 81%); face-to-face lay interviewers, households and group quarters, nobody in both surveys; pooled and restricted to people born in the USA aged 57 or younger (18–57); combined n = 53,238.

Five 10-year birth cohorts: 1974–1983 n = 5,845; 1964–1973 n = 13,555; 1954–1963 n = 16,329; 1944–1953 n = 12,906; 1934–1943 n = 4,603 (they sum to 53,238, my addition); 5-year groupings gave similar results.

anchors.locator: Method › Statistical Analysis, 2nd and 5th paragraphs; Table 2 footnote a
anchors.extracted: All ages come from the single interview. People were at risk of a first drink from age 5, of dependence from the age of their first drink, and of treatment from the age dependence began, and were censored at current age. Covariates were survey, race/ethnicity, income, education and urbanicity, plus age at first drink in the dependence and treatment models. The text says age was tested and not retained, but Table 2 footnote a lists age among the controls (internal inconsistency).

anchors.locator: Results › Table 1, Age at Initiation of Use column (Total sample, Cohort 1 and Cohort 5 rows); Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort › Alcohol use initiation, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Mean age at first drink among people who had drunk (unadjusted means, t tests): men 17.8 (SE 0.03, n = 19,549) vs women 19.0 (SE 0.04, n = 19,263), ratio 0.94, p<0.001; born 1934–1943, 19.1 vs 22.1 (gap 3.0 years); born 1974–1983, 17.1 vs 17.5 (gap 0.4 years); women later in every cohort (cohort 1 t = −2.80, p = 0.007; the others p<0.001).

anchors.locator: Results › Table 2, Time From Use to Dependence column (N=38,309); Figure 2 title; Results › Multivariate Results: Effect of Birth Cohort and Gender › Gender difference, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Cox hazard ratios, men vs women, for alcohol dependence among 38,309 lifetime drinkers (alcohol use defined as more than 12 drinks ever): born 1974–1983 1.56 (95% CI 1.35–1.79), 1964–1973 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1954–1963 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1944–1953 1.79 (1.58–2.02), 1934–1943 1.71 (1.34–2.20). Main effect of gender on dependence F = 223.2, df = 1, p<0.001. These are hazards among everyone at risk, so they combine the chance of dependence with its timing.

anchors.locator: Results › Table 1, Time From Use to Dependence column; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort › Time from initiation to dependence onset, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Mean years from first drink to dependence among people who became dependent (unadjusted): total men 5.8 (SE 0.12, n = 4,631) vs women 5.6 (SE 0.15, n = 3,121), ratio 1.04, not significant. Born 1964–1973: 4.2 (0.16) vs 3.7 (0.16), ratio 1.14, t = 2.36, p = 0.02. Born 1954–1963: 6.4 (0.21) vs 5.5 (0.31), ratio 1.16, not marked significant (my t ≈ 0.9/√(0.21²+0.31²) = 2.40). In the other three cohorts men's mean was shorter, not significantly (2.8 vs 3.1; 7.9 vs 8.6; 10.4 vs 11.8).

anchors.extracted: Cox hazard ratios, men vs women, for first alcohol treatment among 8,564 people with dependence (the 258 first treated before dependence began were excluded): born 1974–1983 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1964–1973 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1954–1963 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1944–1953 1.20 (0.91–1.58), 1934–1943 1.38 (0.84–2.26). Overall gender effect on treatment F = 22.7, df = 1, p<0.001.

anchors.locator: Results › Table 1, Time From Dependence to Treatment Initiation column; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort › Time from dependence onset to first treatment utilization, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Mean years from dependence to first treatment among people treated after onset. Born 1934–1943: men 23.5 (SE 0.91, n = 160) vs women 19.4 (SE 1.42, n = 65), ratio 1.21; the text gives t = 3.2, p = 0.002, while the table footnote marks p<0.001. Total: men 7.0 (0.28, n = 2,088) vs women 6.1 (0.37, n = 968), ratio 1.15, p<0.05. The cohort means run 5.4–23.5 years (men) and 5.1–19.4 (women), so the totals cannot be averages of the rows (n-weighted about 14.8 and 13.2, my calculation).

anchors.locator: Abstract › Conclusions; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Authors' conclusion: a telescoping effect is not evident in the general population, and a complete telescoping effect is not apparent. The Discussion says women had a later first drink but were faster on neither step, by survival curves and mean times, and that telescoping 'disappears when all individuals at risk are considered'. Table 1 shows women significantly faster on mean time to dependence in the 1964–1973 cohort and on mean time to treatment in the 1934–1943 cohort and in the total, so the statement that women were faster on neither step goes beyond the table.

anchors.locator: Results › Multivariate Results: Three-Way Interaction of Gender, Birth Cohort, and Time to Event on Event Hazard, 1st paragraph; Results › Bivariate Results: Survival Curves by Gender and Birth Cohort › Gender difference (after Figure 2), 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Significant cohort x gender x time interaction for time from first drink to dependence (F = 54.08, df = 6, p<0.01). From its direction (data not shown) and from the survival curves (log-rank 46.7 to 181.8, all p<0.01), the authors conclude that men reached dependence faster than women in every cohort, with the gap widening in recent cohorts. The claim reads the hazard ratios as mostly men's higher chance of ever becoming dependent. That is the editors' inference, not the authors'; it fits Table 1, where 4,631/19,549 = 23.7% of men and 3,121/19,263 = 16.2% of women who drank became dependent (ratio 1.46, unweighted, my arithmetic).

Telescoping was reported in clinical samples (refs 1–6, among them Piazza 1989 and Randall 1999): women started drinking later but progressed faster to dependence and, once dependent, to treatment. Research had focused on people in treatment, and whether it happens in the general population was unknown.

Limitations: older respondents reported events from years before the interview, and retrospective reports of drinking history are imperfect. A recall-bias check found that, within a cohort, the prevalence of dependence beginning at 25 or older did not differ between the two surveys. Only 24.6% of people with dependence had ever used any alcohol treatment, so power to detect small cohort differences in treatment was low.

claims.note: All Keyes numbers check: n 8,564, the five treatment hazard ratios and intervals (significant only for 1964–1973 and 1954–1963), 24.6%, and 19.4 vs 23.5. Three precision points. (1) The 8,564 excludes 258 people first treated before dependence began (Table 2 footnote d). (2) Adjustment: Table 2 footnote a also lists age, while the Methods text says age was dropped. (3) The pooled gender effect on treatment was significant (F = 22.7, p<0.001), and log-rank tests were significant in three cohorts (1964–1973, 1954–1963 and 1944–1953). The claim could add these. The 24.6% is not stated as weighted; the unweighted count of people treated after onset is 3,056 of 8,564 = 35.7% (my arithmetic), so the card's 'about 36%' is right. 'Less likely, or slower' is the right reading of a hazard among everyone at risk.

anchors.extracted: Cox hazard ratios, men vs women, for first alcohol treatment among people with dependence: born 1974–1983 1.16 (95% CI 0.77–1.76), 1964–1973 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1954–1963 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1944–1953 1.20 (0.91–1.58), 1934–1943 1.38 (0.84–2.26). anchors.locator: Results › Multivariate Results: Effect of Birth Cohort and Gender › Gender difference, 1st paragraph; Results › Bivariate Results: Survival Curves by Gender and Birth Cohort › Gender difference (after Figure 3), 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Men had a higher hazard of alcohol treatment overall (F = 22.7, df = 1, p<0.001). Survival curves show a shorter time to first treatment in men in the 1964–1973, 1954–1963 and 1944–1953 cohorts (log-rank 15.1, 19.5 and 7.0, p<0.01), and no gender difference in the 1974–1983 and 1934–1943 cohorts.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph; Results › Table 1, Time From Dependence to Treatment Initiation column (Total sample N)
anchors.extracted: 24.6% of people with alcohol dependence in the pooled data had ever used any type of alcohol treatment, said to be consistent with national estimates; the authors say the study lacked power for small cohort differences in treatment. Table 1 counts 2,088 men and 968 women treated after onset, 3,056 of 8,564 = 35.7% unweighted (my arithmetic); the paper does not say whether 24.6% is weighted.

anchors.locator: Results › Table 1, Cohort 5 (born 1934–1943) row, Time From Dependence to Treatment Initiation; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort › Time from dependence onset to first treatment utilization, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Among people treated after onset, born 1934–1943: mean years from dependence to first treatment, women 19.4 (SE 1.42, n = 65) vs men 23.5 (SE 0.91, n = 160), t = 3.2, p = 0.002 (table footnote: p<0.001). These are unadjusted means among people who reached treatment.

anchors.locator: Method › Sources of Data, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Method › Statistical Analysis, 2nd and 5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Pooled NLAES 1991–1992 and NESARC 2001–2002, US-born, aged 18–57. Ages at dependence onset and at first treatment were recalled at one interview. People were at risk of treatment from dependence onset and censored at current age. Covariates were survey, race/ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink.

The authors found limited evidence of a cohort effect on time from dependence to treatment and no gender x cohort or gender x cohort x time interaction for it. They suggest, without testing it, that access, for example through health insurance, matters more than gender norms for treatment.

key_findings.correction: Minor: the log-rank 37.7 (cohort 1 later to first drink than cohort 2) is the men's comparison; the paper says only that results in women were analogous.

The authors do not attribute the narrowing gap to weaker social restraints. They say the convergence is consistent with the possibility that protective social factors have diminished, list supporting research, and note that no formal test exists (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Write 'suggest, as a possibility', not 'attribute'. The recommendations (7th paragraph) are confirmed.

reporting_issues.note: 2,634 > 2,553 confirmed, and the column sums (19,549 and 19,263) agree with the totals. Calling the cohort-1 women's share 'out of line' is a judgment: 1,667/3,292 = 50.6%, against 55.7–69.3% in the other cohorts.
My n-weighted row means are 14.78 (men) and 13.16 (women); cohorts 3–5 hold 770+561+160 = 1,491 treated men; 7.0/6.1 = 1.15.
My approximations give t = 2.40 for cohort 3 and 2.21 for cohort 2 (reported 2.36).
The Results paragraphs on the cohort effect and the two-way interaction also say age was controlled.
The two-way terms have df = 4, consistent with a five-level cohort by gender term; the three-way terms have df = 6 with no explanation.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence suits a descriptive analysis of two probability surveys, and the partial-yes items are documented. Moderate is fair: good frames and response rates, against recalled timing, an estimand that is not the speed among those who reach each step, inconsistent denominators and an unclear age adjustment.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is fair: the abstract's new claim rests on 'data not shown', and the Discussion's summary goes beyond Table 1. Point (1) of the gap is the editors' inference. It is well founded on Table 1 (23.7% of men vs 16.2% of women who drank became dependent, unweighted), but when the claim uses it, the claim should label it as the editors' reading and report the authors' opposite reading.
